## Proof

**Yes**, such a measurable set exists. We construct one explicitly.

Let $C \subseteq [0,1]$ denote the standard middle-thirds Cantor set. Recall that $C$ is closed, has Lebesgue measure $m(C)=0$, and is uncountable (in fact $|C| = 2^{\aleph_0}$).

For each ordered pair of rationals $(p,q)$ with $p<q$, define a scaled, translated copy of $C$ sitting inside $(p,q)$:
$$C_{p,q} \;=\; \{\,p + (q-p)\,x : x \in C\,\} \;\subseteq\; (p,q).$$
Each $C_{p,q}$ is closed, has measure $m(C_{p,q})=(q-p)\,m(C)=0$, and is uncountable.

Now set
$$A \;=\; \bigcup_{\substack{p,q\in\mathbb{Q}\\ p<q}} C_{p,q}.$$

**Measurability.** There are only countably many rational pairs $(p,q)$ with $p<q$, so $A$ is a countable union of closed sets — hence Borel, in particular Lebesgue measurable.

**Measure of $A$.** By countable subadditivity,
$$m(A) \;\le\; \sum_{\substack{p,q\in\mathbb{Q}\\p<q}} m(C_{p,q}) \;=\; 0,$$
so $m(A)=0$.

**$A\cap I$ is uncountable for every open interval $I$.** Let $I=(a,b)$ with $a<b$. Pick rationals $p,q$ with $a<p<q<b$ (possible since $\mathbb{Q}$ is dense in $\mathbb{R}$). Then
$$C_{p,q}\subseteq(p,q)\subseteq I \quad\text{and}\quad C_{p,q}\subseteq A,$$
so $A\cap I \supseteq C_{p,q}$, which is uncountable. Hence $|A\cap I|$ is uncountable.

**$A^{\complement}\cap I$ is uncountable for every open interval $I$.** Since $m(A)=0$,
$$m\!\left(A^{\complement}\cap I\right) \;=\; m(I)-m(A\cap I) \;=\; m(I)-0 \;=\; m(I) \;>\; 0.$$
Any set of positive Lebesgue measure is uncountable, so $|A^{\complement}\cap I|$ is uncountable.

**Conclusion.** The set $A$ is Lebesgue measurable, and for every open interval $I$, both $A\cap I$ and $A^{\complement}\cap I$ are uncountable. $\blacksquare$
